title: How to Save for a House Deposit on a Low Income
description: How to save for a house deposit on a low income: set a realistic target, automate saving, cut big costs, grow income and use first-buyer programs.
keywords: how to save for a house deposit save for a down payment low income first home buyer deposit lifetime isa fha loan
takeaways: You often do not need 20% down. Many first buyers start with 3% to 5%, depending on the country and the loan.
Set a target you can picture, automate the saving, and cut the biggest costs before the small ones.
Keep the deposit separate from your emergency fund, and avoid new debt while you save.
body:
A house deposit can feel like a number that belongs to other people. When rent takes most of your pay and groceries keep getting dearer, saving five figures sounds like a joke. It is a long project, and most advice skips the part that matters: you do not need 20 percent. In the US, some buyers put down 3 percent or 3.5 percent. In the UK, a Lifetime ISA adds a 25 percent bonus to your savings. In Australia, eligible first home buyers can buy with 5 percent. This guide shows you how to save for a house deposit on a low income: how to set a real target, how much to save each month, and which programs can shrink the number you are aiming at.

## What is a house deposit?

A house deposit, also called a down payment, is the chunk of the purchase price you pay upfront from your own savings. The mortgage covers the rest. A bigger deposit usually means a smaller loan and lower monthly payments, but you do not have to wait until you have 20 percent. Many first buyers start with far less, and the right low-deposit loan or government program can make a small deposit work.

## How much deposit do you need to buy a house?

There is no single right number. It depends on your country, your lender, and the loan you use. The old rule was 20 percent, and it still has one real advantage: with 20 percent down you usually skip mortgage insurance. But 20 percent is a target, not a rule.

The table below shows what different deposit sizes look like on one illustrated price. This is an illustration with made-up numbers. Use your own local prices when you set your target.

| Deposit size | Deposit on a $250,000 home | What it usually means                                    |
|------------------|---------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| 3%               | $7,500                         | US HomeReady loans allow as little as 3% for eligible buyers |
| 3.5%             | $8,750                         | US FHA loans allow as low as 3.5%                            |
| 5%               | $12,500                        | Common first-buyer target in the UK and Australia            |
| 10%              | $25,000                        | A mid-range deposit that often brings better loan terms      |
| 20%              | $50,000                        | Usually avoids mortgage insurance                            |

On top of the deposit, budget for closing costs. These are the lender fees, appraisal, title, insurance, and prepaid taxes you pay when the purchase closes. They vary by country and lender, so ask your lender for a written estimate early, and keep this money separate from your deposit fund.

## Step 1: Set a target number you can actually picture

A vague goal like save for a house someday does not survive contact with a rent bill. A number does. Start with the price of homes you would really buy in the area you want to live in. Then pick a deposit percentage your loan allows, and multiply.

Say homes near you sell for around $250,000 and you plan for 5 percent. Your deposit target is $12,500. That number is your finish line. Everything after this step is about closing the gap between that number and zero.

## Step 2: Work out what you can save each month

Saving starts with your real numbers, not a percentage from a chart. Take your monthly take-home pay, subtract your essentials, and subtract your debt minimums.

Here is an illustration with made-up numbers. Say your take-home pay is $2,400 a month. Essentials cost $1,900, and a debt minimum takes $80. That leaves $420. You might save $300 toward the deposit and keep $120 for fun money. If you need help building this monthly picture, [how to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) walks through the order: essentials first, minimums next, then goals.

If nothing is left after essentials and minimums, the answer is not more willpower. The answer is a bigger income, a lower housing cost, or a lower deposit target through a program.

## Step 3: Make the saving automatic

Willpower runs out. Automation does not. Set up a transfer that moves money to your deposit fund on payday, before you have a chance to spend it. Start with an amount you can keep every month, even a small one. A transfer you keep beats a big one you cancel.

Keep the deposit in a separate savings account, not your everyday checking account. Money that sits next to your spending money gets spent. Many savers name the account something plain, like House deposit, so every time they open the app they see the goal. Do not invest deposit money in anything that can drop in value. You need this money to be there when you buy.

## Step 4: Cut the big costs first

Small leaks matter, but the big costs move your timeline most. Housing is usually the biggest one. If you can share a place, take a smaller room, or move somewhere cheaper for a year or two, the saving can be hundreds of dollars a month. Transport is often next: a cheaper car, public transport, or carpooling can free up real money.

Then look at the smaller stuff. Subscriptions you forgot about, food delivery, and impulse buys add up quietly. [How to stop impulse spending](/blog/how-to-stop-impulse-spending/) has a simple waiting rule that helps here. But keep perspective: cutting $150 a month in rent saves $1,800 a year, while cutting a $12 subscription saves $144. Do the big cuts first.

## Step 5: Grow the income side

Cutting only goes so far. At some point the fastest way to reach your target is more money coming in. Extra shifts, overtime, a second job, or a side hustle can all shorten the timeline. Selling things you no longer need can give the fund a one-off boost. [Side hustles for students](/blog/side-hustles-for-students-zero-investment/) has ideas that cost nothing to start.

An extra $200 a month is $2,400 a year. An extra $400 a month is $4,800 a year. That is the difference between a five-year plan and a three-year plan on many targets. Two warnings: do not burn yourself out for a house, and send the extra money straight to the deposit fund.

## Step 6: Use programs that lower the bar

You may not need to save as much as you think. Several countries run programs that let buyers start with a small deposit. Rules change, so check the official pages before you rely on any of them.

### United States

In the US, two routes help low-income buyers. FHA loans let buyers put down as little as 3.5 percent of the purchase price, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development ([U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Loans](http://www.hud.gov/helping-americans/loans)). Fannie Mae's HomeReady program allows as little as 3 percent down for buyers whose income is generally at or below 80 percent of the area median income, with a minimum credit score of 620 ([Bankrate, Guide to Fannie Mae's HomeReady Mortgage Program](http://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/homeready/)). Ask your lender about state down payment assistance programs too.

### United Kingdom

In the UK, a Lifetime ISA is built for this exact job. You can pay in up to 4,000 pounds a year, and the government adds a 25 percent bonus, up to 1,000 pounds a year, according to GOV.UK ([GOV.UK, Lifetime ISA](https://www.gov.uk/lifetime-isa)). You must be 18 to 39 to open one, and the account must have been open for at least 12 months before you use it to buy a first home costing 450,000 pounds or less. Take money out for another reason and you pay a 25 percent withdrawal charge, which can leave you with less than you put in.

### Australia

In Australia, the Australian Government 5% Deposit Scheme lets eligible first home buyers purchase with a 5 percent deposit, and eligible single parents with a 2 percent deposit, without paying lenders mortgage insurance ([Housing Australia, Home ownership a reality for over 300,000 Australians supported by the Australian Government 5% Deposit Scheme](https://www.housingaustralia.gov.au/media/home-ownership-reality-over-300000-australians-supported-australian-government-5-deposit)). Since October 2025 the scheme has no income caps and unlimited places. The guarantee is not cash toward your purchase. If you are in Canada, check current federal first-home buyer programs before you set your target, because the rules differ by country.

## Step 7: Keep the deposit safe and your credit clean

Two habits protect everything you have saved. First, keep an emergency fund separate from your deposit. A car repair or a medical bill should come out of the emergency fund, not the deposit, or one bad month can undo a year of saving. Second, keep your credit in good shape. Pay every bill on time and keep credit card balances low,. [How to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/) explains how to start a small buffer, and [how to build credit from scratch](/blog/how-to-build-credit-from-scratch/) covers the credit side for US readers.

Do not take on new debt while you save for a deposit. A new car loan or a maxed-out card can shrink the mortgage a lender will offer you, even if your deposit fund looks healthy.

## How long will it take? A worked timeline

This is an illustration with made-up numbers. Say your target is $12,500, which is 5 percent of an illustrated $250,000 home. Here is how the timeline changes with your monthly saving:

| Monthly saving | Months to reach $12,500 | About         |
|--------------------|------------------------------|-------------------|
| $200              | 63                           | Just over 5 years |
| $350              | 36                           | 3 years           |
| $500              | 25                           | Just over 2 years |

The math is simple: $200 times 63 is $12,600, $350 times 36 is $12,600, and $500 times 25 is $12,500. Interest and bonuses would change these numbers a little. The point is not the exact month. The point is that the timeline is a number you control. Raise the monthly amount, or lower the target through a program, and the wait shrinks.

## What if the numbers still do not work?

Sometimes the honest answer is that the target is out of reach right now. That is not failure. It is information. You have three levers: a cheaper home, a smaller deposit through a program, or more time. A smaller home in a cheaper area can cut the target by thousands. A low-deposit program can cut the percentage you need.

Other paths exist too. Buying with a partner can combine two deposits and two incomes. In the UK, Shared Ownership lets you buy a share of a home and pay rent on the rest. And some buyers get help from family, but ask your lender first whether a documented gift can count toward the deposit, because the rules depend on the loan.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much deposit do I need to buy a house?

It depends on your country and your loan. In the US, 3 percent or 3.5 percent is possible with the right program. In the UK, 5 percent is a common first-buyer target. In Australia, eligible first home buyers can buy with 5 percent under the government scheme. Twenty percent avoids mortgage insurance, but it is not required.

### How long does it take to save a house deposit?

It depends on your target and your monthly saving. On a $12,500 target, saving $350 a month takes about three years. Saving $500 a month takes just over two years. The worked timeline above shows the trade-off. Raising your monthly amount or lowering your target through a program shortens the wait.

### Can I buy a house with a 3% deposit?

In the US, yes, if you qualify. Fannie Mae's HomeReady program allows 3 percent down for buyers whose income is generally at or below 80 percent of the area median income. In other countries the minimums differ, so check the rules where you plan to buy.

### Should I pay off debt or save for a deposit first?

High-interest debt usually comes first, because the interest can cost more than your savings earn. Keep making minimum payments on everything, attack the most expensive debt, and save a smaller amount toward the deposit at the same time.

### Is it better to wait until I have 20%?

Not always. Waiting can take years, and home prices may rise while you wait. A smaller deposit means a bigger loan and usually mortgage insurance, which costs extra each month. But it can get you into a home years sooner.

## Your next step

Pick one number this week: your deposit target. Then set up one automatic transfer on payday, even if it is small. A target, a transfer, and a program. That is the whole plan to save for a house deposit on a low income.

This article is general information, not personal financial advice. Mortgage and savings rules differ by country, and lenders set their own terms, so check the official pages and speak to a qualified professional before you apply.
